prompt: A game uses AI for its computer-controlled characters. Describe what is meant by artificial intelligence.
points: Computers simulate intelligent behaviour.
Data and rules govern how the data is used.
A computer can learn.
It can adapt.
It can reason or make decisions.
model: AI lets computers simulate intelligent behaviour. It uses data and rules and can learn from experience.
trap: Any three distinct ideas. “Computer” and “intelligent” alone do not create two separate points; do not just repeat “smart”.

prompt: A search engine has the ability to learn. Identify three OTHER AI characteristics.
points: It collects data.
It has rules for using the data.
It can reason.
It can adapt.
model: It collects data, uses rules to process that data, and can reason.
trap: Learning has already been supplied. Repeating it earns no additional point here. This scheme treats data collection and rules as separate points.

prompt: Machine learning belongs to which branch of computer science?
points: Artificial intelligence (AI).
trap: Give the branch, rather than an application or a device.

prompt: Robots can automatically adapt their own processes. Name this ability.
points: Machine learning.

prompt: An expert system already has an inference engine. Identify its three OTHER core components.
points: Knowledge base.
Rule base.
Interface.
trap: Do not repeat the component given in the question. Cambridge accepts “interface”; “user interface” is precise.

prompt: Describe the role of the inference engine in an expert system.
points: It makes decisions.
It applies rules or logic to facts or knowledge.
It produces a result or diagnosis.
model: The inference engine applies the rules to the facts in the knowledge base to produce a diagnosis.
trap: Any two. Naming the component without what it does is not a description.

prompt: The rule base and inference engine are given. Name the other TWO core components.
points: Interface.
Knowledge base.

prompt: Describe the role of the rule base in an expert system.
points: Stores the system’s rules.
The inference engine uses those rules.
The rules link facts in the knowledge base.
model: The rule base stores rules which the inference engine uses to link the facts in the knowledge base.
trap: Any two. Facts belong in the knowledge base; applying rules is the engine’s job.

prompt: An expert system diagnoses faults in a robot vacuum. Select exactly THREE components from: knowledge base, operating system, firewall, server, printer, actuator, inference engine, rule base, encryption.
points: Knowledge base.
Inference engine.
Rule base.
trap: Exactly three selections. A printer or actuator can be hardware used by a wider system, but is not one of these expert-system components.

prompt: Complete the expert-system paragraph using the word bank. Some terms are distractors.
points: A: knowledge base.
B: inference engine.
C: rule base.
D: knowledge base.
E: interface.
trap: One mark per blank. C and D can be reversed in the official scheme: applying the two together is accepted. Do not use “question base” or “mechanical engine”.

prompt: A car with faulty brakes arrives at a garage. Explain how its expert system operates to help diagnose the fault.
points: The user enters evidence/answers through the interface (or connects the car through it).
The inference engine selects questions.
Question selection uses previous answers.
The inference engine decides a diagnosis.
It compares input with the knowledge base and rule base.
It can calculate the most likely option where there are several.
The interface displays the result.
An explanation system can show how it reached the diagnosis.
model: The mechanic enters braking symptoms through the interface. The inference engine chooses questions using previous answers. It compares that evidence with expert facts and applies stored rules to decide a diagnosis. The interface displays the diagnosis.
trap: Any five, not all eight. A list of component names alone is too thin. Apply the process to the braking fault.

prompt: A doctor has already entered symptoms through an interface. A diagnosis will be output. Describe how the expert system DECIDES that diagnosis.
points: An inference engine is used.
It chooses the next questions.
Its question choice depends on earlier input.
It compares symptoms with the knowledge base.
It applies the rule base to the knowledge base to determine the diagnosis.
model: The inference engine chooses further questions from the previous symptom answers, compares those symptoms with the knowledge base and applies the rule base to determine a diagnosis.
trap: Any three. Input and output have been given; focus on processing. Do not assume that writing “the doctor types” again earns a point.

prompt: The garage’s expert system also has machine-learning capabilities. Describe what these capabilities mean.
points: Machine learning is a form of AI.
It can change its own processes/algorithms.
It can change its own data.
It can be trained.
Training can be supervised or unsupervised.
It can learn with or without human interaction.
It analyses patterns and records successful/unsuccessful results to affect later decisions.
For supervised learning, the user supplies both input and desired output.
For unsupervised learning, input is supplied and the system works out the output.
model: Machine learning is part of AI. The system can be trained using examples and can automatically change its own processes and data. It can also record successful and unsuccessful results to influence later decisions.
trap: Any four. This actual four-mark question needs more than “it learns”. Supervised/unsupervised details are accepted alternatives, not compulsory in every answer.

prompt: Explain how a robot vacuum cleaner can use machine learning.
points: It gathers data during vacuuming.
It uses that data to adapt its own processes.
It learns where obstacles are in the room.
It learns which areas are dirtier.
It learns a path through a room.
It learns the shape of a room.
It learns the most efficient cleaning route.
It learns areas to avoid or concentrate on, or which tools to use.
model: It collects data about obstacles while cleaning, uses that data to adapt its route, and avoids those obstacles on later runs.
trap: Any three. Link specific data to a changed future action, rather than “cleans better”.

prompt: A robot must navigate puzzles containing paths, obstacles and dead ends. Explain how its program can use AI.
points: It can use machine-learning algorithms.
It collects data about places it has visited.
It collects obstacle/problem data.
It stores successful actions.
It stores unsuccessful actions.
It identifies or stores patterns.
It avoids repeating the same unsuccessful route.
It knows how to respond to an obstacle next time.
It knows which action is most likely to work next time.
model: It collects data about visited paths and obstacles. It stores which actions succeeded and which led to dead ends. It identifies route patterns and uses them to avoid the failed route next time.
trap: Any four. A sensor–processor–motor chain alone does not explain learning. Refer to stored experience and later decisions.

prompt: Explain how a search engine uses machine learning to improve the relevance of its results.
points: It changes its data or rules.
Changes depend on feedback/results.
It records an unsuitable response.
Next time it changes that result.
Later search results become more relevant/accurate.
It may use supervised/unsupervised learning.
model: The search engine records when its results are unsuitable. It uses that feedback to change its ranking rules, so later searches return more relevant results.
trap: Any three. Merely searching a database or matching keywords does not show learning.

prompt: Explain how a weather system can use machine learning to predict future weather.
points: It can adapt its own data/processes.
It analyses weather data for trends or patterns.
It uses those patterns to predict future weather.
It receives feedback on predictions.
It changes later predictions based on feedback.
It learns what weather occurs at certain times of year.
It uses that seasonal pattern to predict weather at the same time in a later year.
It adapts its weather-prediction rules/processes.
model: The system analyses historical weather data for seasonal patterns, uses them to predict future weather, and changes later predictions using feedback on their accuracy.
trap: Any three. Collecting sensor readings alone is not a complete account of prediction.

prompt: Explain how a smart speaker can use machine learning to improve voice-command input.
points: Collects voice samples or asks people to say different words.
Identifies patterns in voice data.
Adapts its own processes.
Learns to identify a particular voice.
Records successful/unsuccessful commands.
Learns alternative ways to request the same thing.
Learns accents/pronunciations from different voices.
It learns by listening to many different voices.
Learns to ignore background noise.
model: It gathers voice samples and identifies pronunciation patterns. It records successful and unsuccessful commands and uses them to adapt its processes, improving recognition of the user’s accent.
trap: Any four. A microphone converting sound into data does not explain how recognition improves.

prompt: Explain how AI can improve the movements and actions of computer-controlled game characters.
points: It uses machine learning.
It collects data about player actions.
It identifies patterns in the player’s movements.
It learns how the player moves.
It predicts the player’s next movement.
It adapts its own movements/processes in response.
It stores successful/unsuccessful moves.
It learns more efficient moves against the player.
model: The game records the player’s actions, identifies repeated movement patterns and predicts the next move so its characters can adapt their response.
trap: Any three. Better graphics and faster hardware do not explain intelligent movement.

prompt: Give THREE ways grocery-delivery robots could use AI.
points: Learn routes to customers.
Learn obstacle positions on routes.
Learn more effective responses to obstacles.
Distinguish paths from roads through reasoning.
Use machine learning.
Identify patterns in route data.
model: They could learn routes to customers, learn obstacle locations, and reason which parts of a route are paths rather than roads.
trap: Give three distinct ways, not three rewordings of “find the route”.
